planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil at a sunny woodland edge or among low scrub, where in nature this hardy wild species grows up through bracken and heathland vegetation for support, flowering the following June and July. It is considerably hardier than modern grandiflorus hybrid gladiolus and, in climates with reasonably dry winters, the corms can be left undisturbed in the ground year-round rather than lifted.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained soil at a sunny to lightly shaded woodland or heathland edge; the Illyrian or wild gladiolus is a tall, hairless perennial native to southern and western Europe and the Mediterranean, bearing upright spikes of six-petalled, reddish-purple to magenta flowers in June and July. It is best known in Britain for a famously isolated relic population scattered through the bracken of the New Forest, at the northern edge of its natural range, where the plants are easily overlooked beneath the surrounding bracken canopy. Considerably hardier and more drought-tolerant than modern hybrid gladiolus, it is well suited to naturalizing in dry, sunny meadow or open woodland-edge plantings alongside other Mediterranean bulbs. Leave foliage to die back naturally after flowering to recharge the corm for the following season.

planting.note: Plant corms in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full sun, mimicking the wet meadows and fen margins of Central Europe where this rare species grows natively. Unlike most gladiolus, which demand sharp drainage, marsh gladiolus tolerates seasonally damp to boggy ground, making it a candidate for the sunny, moist margins of a bog garden. Because it is legally protected across much of its native range, only nursery-propagated corms of documented cultivated origin should ever be planted.

directions: Plant corms in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; marsh gladiolus is a slender, unbranched perennial native to Central Europe, with a scattered, relict distribution extending to the Balkans. It bears loose spikes of three to six rosy-violet to magenta flowers from May through July and is pollinated by bumblebees. It is among Europe's rarest and most endangered gladiolus species, inhabiting wet meadows and fen margins and carrying protected status under European conservation law. In the garden it is suited to naturalistic wet-meadow or fen-edge plantings paired with other damp-loving perennials, and unlike most gladiolus it should never be allowed to dry out completely during the growing season.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in sharply well-drained clay or sandy soil in full sun; like many South African species gladiolus from winter-rainfall and seasonally dry habitats, it grows through the cooler months, flowers in spring, then goes summer dormant and prefers to stay dry. It is well suited to container culture, where dry summer dormancy is easiest to control, and performs best where winters are mild, zones 8-10.

directions: Plant corms in sharply well-drained clay or sandstone-derived soil in full sun; orchid-flowered sword lily bears loose spikes of five to twelve unusually shaped, greenish to purple flowers marked with dark purple blotches on the lower tepals, flowering in spring. The flowers are very fragrant, a trait shared with only a handful of other gladiolus species. Native across a wide range of clay and sandstone soils from Namibia through the Cape Flats to the Free State, it is drought-tolerant once established and prefers to be kept dry during summer dormancy. A good candidate for a sunny raised bed, rock garden, or pot alongside other winter-growing Cape bulbs.

planting.note: Plant corms in a sheltered, well-drained site; unlike most garden crocosmia, this species is winter-growing, producing leaves through the cooler months and needing protection from hard frost while in leaf. In cultivation outside its native range it typically leafs up late in the year and flowers in spring, rather than following the late-summer bloom pattern of the common hybrid montbretias.

directions: Plant corms in a sheltered, well-drained site in full sun; Namaqualand crocosmia is an unusually tall species restricted in the wild to a few locally moist spots within the arid, winter-rainfall Namaqualand region of northwest South Africa, where it flowers in August and September and is pollinated by sunbirds. Erect stems carry two to four branches bearing up to twenty-two long-tubed, orange-scarlet flowers, the lower tepals sometimes marked with a narrow red median streak. Because it is a winter grower rather than following the usual summer growth cycle of garden crocosmia, it needs a sheltered position and frost protection while actively in leaf, and is best suited to mild, dry-winter climates or container culture where its unconventional seasonal cycle can be managed.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring, or plant container specimens 3-4 inches deep in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained, preferably sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. A narrow endemic of forest edges in Mpumalanga, South Africa, it tolerates considerably more shade than most garden crocosmia and is well suited to a woodland-edge border with reliably moist soil.

directions: Plant in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Mathew's montbretia is a tall South African species, reaching five to eight feet, native to light shade along forest edges and well-drained sandy, boulder-strewn ground in Mpumalanga province. Four- to seven-branched stems carry drooping flower spikes that become horizontal as the bright orange, zygomorphic flowers open from summer into early autumn. Its height and shade tolerance make it a distinctive choice for the back of a partly shaded border or a woodland-edge planting where most crocosmia would struggle, though it is less commonly available than the popular garden hybrids.
